notes.title: 아저씨 and 아줌마
notes.text: Koreans call a middle-aged man 아저씨 and a middle-aged woman 아줌마 (more polite: 아주머니). Shop staff call customers 손님. Young staff are often 알바 (part-timers, from the German "Arbeit").

notes.title: Counters
notes.text: Korean counts things with a counter word after the number: 사과 두 개 (two apples), 고양이 한 마리 (one cat), 책 세 권 (three books), 커피 한 잔 (one cup of coffee). 개 works for most things when you forget the right counter.

notes.title: Korean money
notes.text: Coins: 10, 50, 100 and 500 won. Bills: 1,000, 5,000, 10,000 and 50,000 won. Prices are counted in 만 (ten thousand): 50,000 won is 오만 원, not "fifty thousand."

notes.title: Polite requests

notes.title: Age in Korea
notes.text: Age decides how people speak to each other, so new acquaintances often ask 몇 살이에요? or which year you were born. Since 2023 Korea officially uses "international age" (만 나이), but many people still count the old way, where you're one at birth. For elders, ask 연세가 어떻게 되세요? instead.

notes.title: Filler words
notes.text: Korean speakers fill pauses with 음…, 그…, 저… and 어… — like "um" and "uh." Using them makes your Korean sound natural while you think.
